Clavis Steganographiae — Modes XXI-XXII, Damage-Preserving Translation

Mode XXI

Mode XXI. It is used with alternating words, with the significant letters transposed into the second [following position].^1

Mode 21. With alternating words set out, of which he treats the first as empty, the second as significant, the third again as empty, [the fourth likewise/significantly: unclear], if they follow one another in sequence up to the end of the proposed narration: the letter which first belonged in the significant word has been transposed into the second following [letter/position]. Thus, for the letter A, C is taken; for B, D is taken [conjectured from rule; OCR reads corruptly]; and so in sequence almost to the end of the alphabet. Further, for X [unclear: perhaps Y], A is taken, and for Z, B.^2 But the character which is not necessary for us in the vernacular name is to be omitted in all the following alphabets [or: in all following uses of the alphabet]; but now rather let us give an example of this mode.

Example XXI

S. D. I would rejoice to answer your letters; so may Christ make me rejoice, I would send the requested volumes, if at last [I/he] had had them. I have been zealous [or: I envied; OCR/grammar damaged] while alive, [unclear] nearest, and he says, in very weighty hidden treatises on good zeal, which the sharpest philosophers have; but I would give you thanks, long immortal [unclear], my father, for having judged that you, by the mutual glory of slight love, unharmed in this business of a familiar mind, most diligently redeemed what was weightier by modesty. I have plainly learned, as it seems, that you, falsely praising, would have thanks no more than the dead; and therefore you are moved [unclear] by his petitions to effect it soon, if our Christian people had [it].

Here among the masters I have nowhere seen a Latin translation of Pico of Mirandola,^3 and yet I confess that I myself have read the [little servant/little book: unclear]. Therefore, lest the serious burdens of the request now be frustrated, [by] the highest truth of Christ, which no darkness hides, and as examiner of hearts,^4 I [wish] to oblige you, not rather to conceal the other [opinions/things: unclear], to gain virtue, to know more things quickly, finally to come forth alive.

Love Christ purely; see that, as far as you can, you exist as a priest in works. Love Christ purely, whom you are ordered to love beyond measure. A true lover of Christ is preserved by zeal for souls,^5 and sets nothing before Christ's command; since in us the zeal of God is the best thing of the soul. The love of blessedness, by loving God the Zealot,^6 truly [animates/is animated: unclear]; for the known saving things of pious observance of the Catholic faith,^7 and giving thanks to almighty God Jesus Christ, who has granted the glorious [unclear] of all things, may he confer on you love for eternity and [unclear] will establish the exalted deeds of Christians. Farewell.

Tenor.

Hidden Tenor

Hidden tenor of the aforesaid.

[See tenor_md; this is the German plaintext concealed by the preceding Latin cipher-example, not the source from which the Latin prose is to be translated.]^8

Mode XXII

Mode XXII. By the transposition of letters already examined, after two idle [words] it places the same number of significant [words].^9

Mode 22. It begins with two idle words and immediately joins two significant ones; thus, through two empty [words] and two significant ones, it alternately carries through the whole open narration and the following [sequence: unclear]. The first letter of every significant word has been placed in the third [following position]; thus for A, D is taken, for B, E is taken, and for C, F is taken. So it follows in order to the end, just as for the first letter of the alphabet A, X is taken [unclear/corrupt], for B [unclear], and for Z, E [unclear]. As the alphabet in secret matters shows, the red [letters/signs] indicate this hidden [voice/utterance].^10

Alphabet: A b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r [unclear] s [unclear] t [unclear] n s x t z / n a x b z. The printed alphabet-line is too damaged to normalize without inventing letters.

When, however, you wish to write in the prescribed way that follows, place the alphabet before you, and look carefully that you keep the prescribed order, lest you make an error for the reader and for yourself. But now let us set down an example of this twenty-second mode, which proceeds by alternating pairs.

Example XXII

S. Since I have known you as a devoted lover of the arts of humanity^11 and a cultivator of the Christian faith, [unclear: macerantem], most blessed of all philosophers [or: most kindly, O philosopher; damaged agreement], I gladly comply with your most urgent requests, brought by wondrous pleasure of friendship. I transmit to you the book, well known, concerning ecclesiastical writers and Catholic doctors,^12 so that you may have [something] by which the mind is [shown/offended: unclear].

The codex [concerning/from] torments [or: engines of war: unclear] in the [book/inequality: unclear] concerning spirits, and whatever glorious poison you have shuddered at in questions, send back to me. I beseech Christ [that] with the eye/zeal of our heart [unclear] you adorn yourself with the most holy [thing] of his love, and that he make you a lover of heavenly goods and exempt from low desires; that you learn to despise vain honors, to turn yourself, so that you may penetrate the sublime things of the art and also the great secrets [the excerpt breaks off].

Tenor (German plaintext concealed by the cipher)

Peter Druncer von Fridburg Labsodel genannt/ trincket gern starcken Wein. Ist Doctor stultorum zu Spanheim gemacht.

Modern English: Peter Druncer of Fridburg, called Labsodel, likes to drink strong wine. He has been made Doctor of Fools at Spanheim.

^1. Mode / Modus: a technical steganographic procedure in Trithemius's system. The heading's final vitiur is an OCR scanno for utitur. ^2. The rule appears to be a Caesar-style alphabetic transposition by two places. The examples after A are OCR-damaged; pro e, accipiatur e cannot stand as printed. x -> a may reflect omission of a letter or OCR loss; not silently normalized. ^3. Pico of Mirandola: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Renaissance philosopher; the Latin has Pici Mirandulani, with damaged surrounding syntax. ^4. Examiner of hearts: theological phrase for Christ/God as knower of inward intentions; here embedded in the cover text. ^5. Zeal for souls: pastoral/theological vocabulary; the passage repeatedly uses zelus as pious cover-language while concealing a German tenor. ^6. God the Zealot: Deum Zelotem; biblical-theological epithet for God as jealous/zealous. The syntax around animaregur is corrupt. ^7. Catholic faith: catholicae fidei; confessional/theological cover vocabulary in the example narrative. ^8. Tenor / tenor occultus: the concealed plaintext message. Here it is German, and must not be flattened into the Latin cover letter. ^9. Idle/vacant vs. significant words: cipher terminology; ociosas/oicioas and vacas denote cover words not carrying the hidden message, while significativae carry cipher-significant letters. ^10. The alphabet line for Mode XXII is substantially corrupt: duplicated/misordered letters such as p s q t r n s x t z are likely OCR or print damage. Reconstruction would require collation. ^11. Arts of humanity: artium humanitatis, i.e. humanist learning or humane letters. ^12. Ecclesiastical writers and Catholic doctors: learned/theological cover vocabulary; the phrase likely alludes to a catalog or book on church authors, but the surrounding text is damaged.

[unclear] we ask to penetrate; and for this [unclear] I have purified a continual desire for glory in the office [or duty], because the Catholic faith^1 always [unclear] at the extremes / from the border, by morals, virtue, and humility [unclear] certain better things of office; joys cast down to fall, not [unclear], so as to please human beings. S. D.^6 The things which I had set before myself to be solved, with Christ^7 helping, I have solved. I would like you to report back to me briefly what this has profited you, what you are doing about the tempters / attempts, and the whole matter. A brother recently reported to me, with a serious friend also then [unclear], a final refused / rejected [unclear] young man [unclear], recounting every invocation of Christ from the dead, and wonderful and dreadful things prepared among the infernal regions^8 for Christians [unclear], narrating their torments [unclear]; [happy?] those who by acting perversely crucified Christ grievously [unclear], especially those who, [though aided] by the kindly benefit of redemption, [unclear], always ungrateful to Christ, with the obediences of penitents neglected [unclear].

[The] joys to come, the pleasure of the world and of those following it, which [unclear] continually and rather negligently gnawing at them, they bitterly feared, was being condemned. Misfortune: we die; we suffer cruel, harsh things, having greedily gulped down earthly and worldly things. We read the commandment [conjectured: of the heart / Corinthians?]; we despised [unclear]; loving iniquity, we receive the recompense of eternal damnation.^9 Alas, unhappy as we are, why do we deny Christ, why have we neglected the time of indulgence! Thus, and many other astonishing things, he reported [unclear], etc. I cannot write more this time, especially in few letters. Farewell.

Mode XXIV

Mode XXIV. It admits all significant words, and transposes each letter into the fifth following one.

Mode 24. After the pattern of the first, it admits all the significant words of its own narrative, and transposes the first letter of each word into the fifth nearest following: namely, so that for a f is taken, for b g, for c h [the OCR reads b], and consequently, as we shall show by counting in the alphabet, where the black letter, placed immediately above, is taken for the red letter.^10

A, f, bg, c, h, di, ak, fl, gm, hn, io, k, p, lq, mr, ns, ot, p, u, q, x, r, z, fa, i b, v, e, x, d, z, e.^4

Therefore, whenever you wish to write or read in this mode, place this alphabet before you, making all the signs for each mode.

Example XXIV

S. By diligent services, establishing the kindness of a benefactor, remember the reproach [unclear] of my benefits, I beseech you by holy charity. In the matters of Zealania^11 good [things] of those people, and the goodness of our Catholic religion, are built up by works, [with] the sanction of those adorning [them] faithfully. But speak kindly, brother, so that fear may be cast off by me, your brother; bilingual persons are even bitter to love, [unclear], and by contention they assert goodness with evil works. With good works also daily [adorn] splendid reputation and steadfastness; adorn and lift up the soul: have insistence / perseverance, continence, and zeal for the name [unclear].

[page break]

For your name: be zealous for the excellent name of friends and brothers, best in goodness; [unclear] by works [unclear] in one case of the body, adorned in every respect, and when there is sickness with a Catholic [unclear]. Farewell.

See tenor_md.

Mode XXV Heading

Mode XXV. After the pattern of the preceding, it admits all significant words, but transposes each one into the sixth.^12

Tenor (German plaintext concealed by the cipher)

Tenor Before Mode XXIII

Was ich dir hab geben zu behalten/ soltu bewahren/ und niemand geben dann mir allein.

Modern English: What I have given you to keep, you shall preserve, and give to no one except to me alone.

Nim. Morgen umb Neun Uhr meiner wahr an der Pforten/ Da wil ich mit 200. Pferden heimlich stills schwiegend erscheinen.

Modern English: Take [note]. Tomorrow at nine o’clock, wait for me at the gate; there I will appear secretly, silently, and without speaking, with 200 horses.

Nicht acht auf meuß Wort / Ich meine es nicht als so harte / es muß stund alsso seyn / durch ursach wil ich dir sagen.

Modern English: Pay no attention to my word[s]. I do not mean it so harshly; it had to be that way for now. I will tell you the reason.

Mode 25

Mode 25, in that preceding total, [conjectured: admits no null word]^1; rather, all the words which it admits are significant,^2 because there is no need to insert any [null words]. Johannes Trithemius,^7 abbot of Sponheim.^8

Example of the hidden secret. [German tenor supplied below.] Let us now compose the narration of this hidden matter.

S.D.^9 A humble [person / statement] [unclear: lamentem] before [unclear] grace of remission, consequently; the grace of redemption restrains freedom; but penitent human beings are freed by the majesty of [unclear: dieris / perhaps Dei]. [Unclear: piffiam falsoator] a king of power [unclear: indicaturne]. Blessedness has promised all joys to those holding divine [things] and Catholic rectitude. Good blessedness [unclear: porcellis] favors those holding the law in freedom; they will rejoice at last, [unclear: s] Catholics. Mode 26

Mode 26. It proceeds by alternate words, and each letter of the significant words is transferred to the second [position].^12

Mode 26 proceeds by alternation in a second way: first a null word is placed at the beginning, then another significant word; afterward again one null word, then another significant word, and so on consequently to the end of the narration. Further, for each letter of the significant words, the first letter which appears to follow in order is to be taken: for A, b is taken; for b, [unclear: i]; for [unclear: e], and so consequently, as will appear in the following alphabet, where the black letters are taken for the value. [Unclear: Eubolig.]

But so that you may easily understand this art and gather the method of composing a secret narration, I shall make the procedure plain with its own letters, joined to [unclear: the seventh / next] transposition, and set it below and show it:

Behalt alle Brieff die ich dir sende heimlich / und lass siemand sehen.

^1. OCR summa vacuam recipit is likely a scanno for nullam vacuam recipit; the sense of the method requires “no null word,” since the next clause says all words are significant. ^2. significativae dictiones: cipher-bearing words, opposed to vacantes, null or filler words. ^3. ars libri huius: the steganographic/cipher procedure taught in the book, not a magical claim to be normalized away. ^4. signa modorum: markers identifying which cipher mode is being used. ^5. in sextam transponuntur sequentem: a substitution/transposition alphabet taking the sixth following letter; the OCR alphabet is badly corrupted. ^6. primas literas significativas: the initial letters that carry the hidden message. ^7. Clavis Steganographiae, Modus XXVI-XXVIII Fragment

Closing Instruction to the Previous Method

[unclear] to interpose, beginning from one vacant [word]^1 [unclear], to which you then convert the first letter of the signifying [conjectured: words]^2, as we shall make easily probable in the second example.

Example XXVI

S. P.^3 I had entrusted my books^4 to you under the condition that they were to be restored, most distinguished [sir], with a thousand [conjectured: good assurances]; but they were by no means to be kept back. Since you ought to have sent them back in a short time, you are acting against law; for, concerning a catholic promise^5 [unclear], do not [unclear: separate?] the condition from the promise made. It does not belong to a good and honorable man [unclear: because of the nobility of greater persons?] to violate a promise. But you had promised that they would be restored very diligently in a short time. It is frivolity to bring forward a promise for the Greek Kalends.^6 Do we not in fact seek, with great goodwill, to promise great things and shamefully repay the smallest things? A promise adorns a soldier^7, nor does it belong to a Christian not to bear/observe a condition. Moreover Christian ordinance commands that a promise be kept, another's property be restored, and that what you desire to be done for you be done in another's case. I do not wish my displayed/exposed books, which I had entrusted to you [unclear: as a supplement?], to be drawn out longer, nor to extend to the Greek Kalends. Release/send back with me my [unclear]; I hold/appeal to the nobility of your most honorable family, Bunnefind^8; consider your stock, [and] send back to me [unclear] my volumes.

Farewell.

The hidden tenor of the above.^9

Method XXVII

Method XXVII. It uses alternate words^10, and any given letter is transferred to the eighth following [letter].^11

Method 27. After one vacant word has been put first, another signifying [word] immediately follows, and so it proceeds consequently by the alternate route. But each letter in any signifying [word] is transferred from the first [position] into its own [conjectured: eighth] position afterward, into the next following [letter]: thus, for the letter A, i is taken; for b, k; for c, l; and so consequently, as the later alphabet more clearly demonstrates.

A i b k c l d m e n f o g p h q i r k s l t m u n x o z p a q b r e s d r e u f x g z h.

To express the consequence of an alphabet of this kind, let us set down an example: so that, in the wording of the secret, the letters [conjectured: moved/shifted]^11 from the signifying words come first; afterward, the example.

R L q f l f m n m i d i m f l b r l q t r v n d f f v d d n x l f f v n m v r u q g n i n r l d s l q d e n l v r t m m v u p n l m o l f x m l i x m n c l d b x m f l f n d x.

Intention of the secret.^9

Example XXVII

S. D.^3 A rumor has gone out concerning the abbot of Limburg^12, who dismissed Brother Fleidersen^13, a faithful man and [conjectured: not inexperienced] in temporal affairs^14, and brought in monks because of need/poverty, assigning them themselves to office. I wonder greatly. When I recall the counsels of the brothers, truly joined with [those] of the Limburgers, [unclear]. In temporal affairs, indeed, [unclear: he was not incapable?]; the same man dismissed a most faithful man, when he reproved [unclear: the holy men?], who ought rather to have said thanks to our savior J. C.^15 for the fidelity of so great a brother, who could have recovered their necessities. Why, I ask, is a good and necessary administrator rejected? What shall I say? I do not praise that the brothers then let go a man most skilled in temporal affairs, who had aided Limburg [unclear: very greatly]. I grieve vehemently that the monks of Limburg so despised [him], who had dismissed an excellent man, and set up monks worth absolutely nothing in temporal affairs; they proved [unclear: most bitter/harsh]. Macharius the abbot^16, it did not befit you so to treat such a man. At first you praised him; now suddenly [you reject] a man much better and to be postponed to none. For Christ is my witness: if I, as becomes a Christian, [unclear: were in your place], I would give the greatest thanks and would take care that he did not depart; [unclear: up to your Christ?] you preferred to let a faithful man, wearied by the counsel of false men, go, lest, after your affairs had been abandoned, he himself [unclear: be of recovering them]. Farewell. From Sponheim.^17 [unclear: Non./Nones?] of Jan[uary]. In the year of the Lord 1499. Joh. Trith. Abb.^18

Method XXVIII

Method XXVIII. In the likeness of the preceding [method], it uses alternate words, and transfers the signifying letter to the ninth [following letter].

Mode 33 and the Opening of Mode 34: Alternating Words and Alphabetic Shifts

The passage explains two steganographic procedures in which alternate cover words carry a hidden message by shifting the first letter of each significant word through a fixed substitution alphabet, followed by German hidden texts, significant-letter strings, and a damaged sample cover letter attributed to Trithemius.

Mode XXXIII

Mode 33, proceeding by alternate words as the preceding modes do, transfers the first significant letter to the fourteenth place.^1

Mode 33 begins the second narrative with one vacant word,^2 and then proceeds by alternate words in turn. For the first significant letter of each word it takes the letter following it in the fourteenth place: thus for A, P is taken; for B, Q; for C, R; and so continuously through the order of the alphabet, as in the alphabet that follows.^3

The Three General Keys of Steganography

The passage explains Trithemius's three general keys for reading the Steganographia: vowel-consonant substitution, null-letter counting rules, a one-letter alphabetic shift, and a partitioning method for concealed text.

General Key of Steganography

The section is headed General Key of Steganography^1 and, in the running page title, attributed to Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.^2 [conjectured: If the vowel a occurs in your secret sense, put the consonant b in its place], and conversely. If the letter b has to be written, write the vowel a in place of b, and proceed in the same way in the remaining modes.^3 For variation these modes are also inverted by retrogradation: for a put g, for e put f, for i put d; since i is the middle term, it always remains fixed and will never be changed.^4 The visible scheme gives the corresponding vowel-consonant substitutions as:

a e i o u
g f d c b
n m l k h
t s r q p

Now, for example, if the word Omnipotens is to be written by the first mode, it is written [conjectured: Fmndpftcns]; by the second, Moulpmtkus; by the third, Smnrasuqno. Conversely, by the three later modes it is written as follows: by the first, [conjectured: Cmndpctfns]; by the second, Kealpktmas; by the third, [conjectured: Qmnruqasne]. In this way we proceed with whole sentences. From these six previously described modes arise the following rules, according to which you will regulate yourself in reading our book; each of the subsequent modes is varied by any one of the rules just described. You will observe the variation of those modes in many parts of our book, especially in the conjurations of demons, where our secrets are concealed and are revealed to those who know our rules and seals.^5

As an example let the following sentence serve you; although it can be written by all the rules already stated, it has pleased us to set it down here by the first mode: Miserere omnipotens Deus animabus famulorum tuorum in te pie requiescentium: 'Have mercy, almighty God, on the souls of your servants who rest piously in you.'^6 By the first mode this sentence becomes: [conjectured: Mdscrcrc fmndpftcns icgs bndmbags obmglfrgm tgfrgm dn tc pdc rcqgdcsccntdgm], etc. Since, because of the lack of vowels, no word meaning anything is supplied here for insertion into our book among so many consonants, we have followed the rule of the following example by taking the aforesaid consonants: [conjectured: Midosa coracir ocafa mini dapofa ticonusa], etc. From these letters only the first letter is significant for you; immediately after it follows a non-significant or vacant letter, and so alternately, as the points marked above the significant letters show.^7

For the sake of abbreviation, all the rules and variations are shown below by numbers. In these examples, whenever 0, the arithmetic sign or zifrum, is placed, it denotes that number of non-significant letters for you; the number immediately following denotes that number of significant letters.^8

First mode: 10 10 10 10 10 10 10 10, etc.

Second mode: 01 01 01 01 01 01 01 01, etc.

Third mode: 200 200 200 200 200 200 200 200, etc.

Fourth mode: [conjectured: 002] [conjectured: 002] [conjectured: 002] [conjectured: 002], etc.

Fifth mode: 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001 0001, etc.

Sixth mode: 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000, etc.

Seventh mode: 0002 0002 0002 0002 0002 0002 0002 0002, etc.

Eighth mode: 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000, etc.

The Second General Key

The second general key is made in this manner: the writer precedes and the reader follows.^9 Thus, in this example, 'Have mercy, almighty God, on the souls of your servants,' etc., becomes: lhrdqdq nlmbprpsdmr edtr zmhlzat ezlkngtfsngtl, etc. Since these letters, joined in this way, signify nothing, they likewise appear in our book enciphered through the preceding eight examples or modes.

The Third and Last General Key

The third and last general key is constructed in this way. If you wished to write 'Have mercy, God,' etc., as above, you will do this: count all the letters of your intended sense and divide them into as many parts as you choose. For example, if you wished to divide them into two parts, for one part of the whole sentence set above you will have forty-five letters; when divided, twenty-two will come to one part, and one remains, which at the end you will always [conjectured: append to the rest].^10

^1. The Clavis generalis is the explanatory 'key' to the Steganographia's hidden-writing procedures. The damaged OCR here corresponds to the Clavis Steganographiae / Clavis generalis triplex tradition; restored readings were checked against Thomas Ernst's online restoration: https://steganographia-ernst.com/. ^2. Johannes Trithemius (1462-1516), Benedictine abbot of Sponheim or Spanheim, composed the Steganographia as a work whose surface language of spirits and conjurations conceals practical cryptographic instructions. ^3. Modus here means a specific cipher procedure, not merely a stylistic 'manner': each mode defines how vowels, consonants, significant letters, and null letters are substituted or counted. ^4. Retrogradation is used in a cipher sense: the substitution pattern is reversed through the displayed series. The statement that i remains fixed reflects its place as the middle vowel in Trithemius's five-vowel scheme. ^5. The 'conjurations of demons' are the notorious cover-text of the Steganographia. In this Clavis, Trithemius presents them as containers for concealed messages, readable by those who know the regulae and sigilla, that is, the governing rules and identifying cipher signs. ^6. Miserere evokes the Vulgate incipit of Psalm 50/51, 'Miserere mei Deus,' but the full sentence here is a liturgical-style prayer for the dead rather than a direct biblical quotation. ^7. Significant letters carry the hidden message; non-significant or vacant letters are nulls. The example inserts vowels and syllabic padding so that an otherwise consonant-heavy cipher stream can be disguised as pronounceable nonsense. ^8. Zifrum, from medieval Latin cifra/zephirum, denotes zero in arithmetic and is historically related to the word 'cipher.' Trithemius uses 0 as a compact notation for null-letter slots. ^9. 'The writer precedes and the reader follows' describes a one-letter alphabetic shift: the writer substitutes the preceding letter, and the reader recovers the plaintext by moving forward one letter. ^10. The third key is a partitioning or transposition rule: the plaintext is counted, divided into chosen parts, and any remainder is carried to the end. The OCR breaks off after semper, so the final action is supplied only as a contextual conjecture.
